stem: A client taking digoxin has a serum potassium level of 3.1 mmol/L, nausea, anorexia, fatigue, and new frequent premature ventricular contractions. Which action should the nurse take?

options.A: Give the scheduled digoxin, continue cardiac monitoring, notify the provider of the low potassium, and recheck potassium later.
options.B: Give digoxin with food, continue cardiac monitoring, notify the provider if vomiting occurs, and reassess the symptoms.
options.C: Withhold digoxin, continue cardiac monitoring, notify the provider, and obtain serum digoxin, electrolytes, and renal function.
options.D: Hold digoxin until potassium is corrected, continue cardiac monitoring, notify the provider, and resume the dose if the ectopy resolves.

rationale: The combination of nausea, anorexia, fatigue, and new premature ventricular contractions is consistent with digoxin toxicity. The current digoxin label identifies hypokalemia as a factor that predisposes to toxicity and directs clinicians to obtain a serum digoxin level when toxicity is suspected, assess electrolytes and renal function, interrupt or discontinue digoxin as appropriate, and use cardiac monitoring. A potassium value of 3.1 mmol/L is below the Mayo Clinic Laboratories adult reference interval of 3.6–5.2 mmol/L. Therefore C is the best answer. A and B give another digoxin dose despite a toxicity pattern. D incorrectly treats correction of potassium and improvement in ectopy as sufficient grounds to resume digoxin without completing the toxicity evaluation.
educational_objective: Recognize suspected digoxin toxicity when gastrointestinal symptoms and ventricular ectopy occur in a client with hypokalemia, and respond by withholding digoxin, maintaining cardiac monitoring, and obtaining current digoxin, electrolyte, and renal-function data while escalating the finding.
source_organization: U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed
source_version_date: DailyMed page updated 2026-01-29; full prescribing information revised 2026-01
source_locator: Full Prescribing Information §§2.5 (Monitoring to Assess Safety, Efficacy, and Therapeutic Blood Levels), 5.3 (Digoxin Toxicity), 10.1 (Signs and Symptoms in Adults and Children), and 10.2 (Treatment — Chronic Overdose)
source_claim_supported: Digoxin toxicity can present with anorexia, nausea, fatigue and ventricular premature contractions; hypokalemia predisposes to toxicity. When toxicity is suspected, obtain serum digoxin data, assess electrolytes and renal function, interrupt/discontinue digoxin as appropriate, and use cardiac monitoring.

source_original.stem: A client taking digoxin and furosemide has a potassium level of 3.1 mEq/L, nausea, anorexia, fatigue, and new frequent premature ventricular contractions. Which action is the nurse's priority?

options.A: Administer the scheduled digoxin, then repeat the potassium level after the next dose of furosemide.
options.B: Hold furosemide only, give the digoxin, and treat the ventricular ectopy as an unrelated rhythm change.
options.C: Withhold digoxin, notify the provider, and obtain current digoxin, electrolyte, and renal-function data.
options.D: Give the digoxin with food and continue routine monitoring because gastrointestinal effects are expected.

source_original.rationale: Nausea, anorexia, fatigue, and ventricular ectopy are compatible with digoxin toxicity, and hypokalemia increases susceptibility. The nurse should withhold digoxin and promptly escalate for a current digoxin level, electrolyte assessment, and renal-function assessment. Giving another dose despite this cluster of findings can worsen toxicity.
source_original.source_detail: Current DailyMed digoxin label reviewed 2026-08-14; Warnings and Precautions §5.3 Digoxin Toxicity, including gastrointestinal and cardiac manifestations and predisposition with hypokalemia.

correction_summary: Removed furosemide because it was not necessary to the tested construct and created an avoidable second medication-management branch. Tightened the item to recognition and immediate management of suspected digoxin toxicity; added cardiac monitoring to the correct response; rebuilt distractors to remain within the same construct; verified the 3.1 mmol/L potassium value against Mayo Clinic Laboratories; expanded the exact DailyMed locator to §§2.5, 5.3, 10.1, and 10.2; changed difficulty from hard to moderate.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — digoxin toxicity recognition and immediate medication-safety response
audit_findings.source_authority: PASS — current official DailyMed prescribing information is the primary pharmacology source; Mayo Clinic Laboratories is used only to verify the serum-potassium reference interval.
audit_findings.currentness: PASS — exact DailyMed set-id checked 2026-08-16; label updated 2026-01-29 and revised 2026-01.
audit_findings.exact_locator: PASS — DailyMed §§5.3 and 10.1 support the symptom/risk pattern; §2.5 supports toxicity monitoring and serum digoxin interpretation; §10.2 supports discontinuing digoxin and cardiac monitoring when toxicity is suspected.

supplementary_lab_source.claim_supported: A serum potassium of 3.1 mmol/L is below the listed reference interval.

audit_findings.stem: PASS after correction — retains the clinically meaningful low potassium, gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue, and ventricular ectopy while removing furosemide as an unnecessary secondary construct.
audit_findings.option_A: Wrong but plausible — focuses on low potassium while still giving digoxin despite a toxicity pattern.
audit_findings.option_B: Wrong but plausible — misclassifies gastrointestinal findings as manageable administration effects and still gives digoxin.
audit_findings.option_C: Correct — withholds digoxin, maintains cardiac monitoring, escalates the finding, and obtains the exact toxicity-related data supported by the label.
audit_findings.option_D: Wrong but plausible — recognizes the potassium problem and withholds digoxin temporarily, but incorrectly assumes potassium correction and rhythm improvement are sufficient to resume therapy without completing toxicity evaluation.
audit_findings.rationale: PASS after rewrite — explains the toxicity pattern, the role of hypokalemia, the immediate response, and why each distractor fails without adding unsupported dosing thresholds or treatment rules.
audit_findings.educational_objective: PASS — specific to recognizing and responding to suspected digoxin toxicity in the presence of hypokalemia and ventricular ectopy.
audit_findings.ambiguity_and_second_answer: PASS — C is the only answer that both avoids further digoxin exposure and performs the full label-supported toxicity evaluation while maintaining cardiac monitoring.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all four options contain comparable multi-step actions and stay within the same digoxin-toxicity construct; no grammatical cue or unique absolute wording identifies C.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN 2026 printed p.12/PDF p.16 explicitly includes review of pertinent data before medication administration and evaluation of client response to medication under Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies.
audit_findings.difficulty: Moderate — requires integration of a low potassium value, gastrointestinal symptoms, fatigue, and ventricular ectopy to identify toxicity and select the safest response; the original 'hard' rating was overstated.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: PASS — independently rechecked current label version, exact locators, potassium reference interval, stem logic, every option, correct answer, rationale, Educational Objective, ambiguity, second-answer risk, cueing, blueprint mapping, and unresolved conflicts from zero.
